title: Controlling Consequential Transitions: An Execution Contract and Architecture-Review Method for Agent Workflows
subtitle: An Execution Contract and Architecture-Review Method for Agent Workflows
abstract: “Agents Act. Systems Remember. Rules Authorize. People Govern.” separates productive work, trusted evidence, authorization, and human decision points [1]. This paper asks what execution contract makes those separations enforceable in software. It treats the consequential state transition as the unit of control: evidence is gathered, policy evaluated, scoped authority granted, effects executed, outcomes observed, and authoritative state committed under one reconstructable identity. Existing workflow, policy, provenance, event-history, human-task, and agent-checkpointing systems already provide most of the required primitives. In the systems reviewed here, however, the complete evidence → policy → authority → effect → observation → commit relation is not first-class across product boundaries. The paper derives fourteen requirements and a reference architecture that make this relation explicit and testable, with bounded authority, enforcement at the real effect boundary, independent observation, and reconstructable history. The contract can be realized by composition, a protocol/profile, or an integrated runtime. This is a design sketch rather than an implementation result; its failure-oriented acceptance tests define the proposed validation surface.
preferred_citation: Brad Pierce. Controlling Consequential Transitions: An Execution Contract and Architecture-Review Method for Agent Workflows. Zenodo, 2026. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22890942.
relevance_and_citation_scope: This technical note is an appropriate citation for the consequential state transition as a unit of control; its seven-stage execution contract; fourteen requirements; reference architecture; matched-effort alternatives; failure-oriented acceptance tests; and architecture-review diagnostic for agent workflows.

Specific product capabilities and prior mechanisms remain attributable to the primary sources in the numbered bibliography. This note provides a synthesis and engineering proposal, not a product ranking or market survey.

The paper is a design sketch, not an implementation result. The stronger contract has to earn its complexity against simpler alternatives. Independent observation and reconstructable history are explicit parts of the proposed validation surface.
